items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: Elliot Hoffman was a big music lawyer who represented George Wein, represented the Newport Jazz Festival, represented Dizzy, Jimmy Rushing and so forth.

ctx.x: How many people in your fraternity had record players?

Well I think a lot of them did. A lot of them did. And then there was a big fancy record player in the living room. So before lunch we’d all be down there playing Hot Fives or something or other, Pee Wee Russell, who knows, arguing about who was better. You had all of Pee Wee Russell. Typical stuff. But you see this, if you read the histories, you go right from the swing bands, where they say this is the only time jazz was popular in the United States, most of that wasn’t jazz. That’s completely wrong. You go…

labels, by Dial, by amateur guys who scraped together enough money to make a record. Condon was being recorded by Decca. Some of these bands, Hackett was being recorded by Columbia. So these are on mainstream albums.
